questions.stem: Jenny, 26, is at her GP with 6 weeks of productive cough, streaks of blood in her sputum, weight loss and right upper lobe opacification on X-ray. Pulmonary TB is suspected. You give her three sputum jars to fill at home. Which instruction is best?
options: Spit saliva into the jar after rinsing your mouth with antiseptic mouthwash
On waking, breathe deeply and cough phlegm up from the chest, outdoors or by a window
Collect all three samples within one hour this afternoon so results come back sooner
Cough into the jar in the small bathroom with the door closed to protect your family
questions.why: A good AFB sample is sputum coughed up from deep in the chest, best collected early in the morning when overnight secretions have built up. She should collect it outdoors or in a well-ventilated space, away from other people, because coughing spreads infectious aerosols.
notes: Saliva does not reliably contain bacilli, so the sample is poor, and antiseptic mouthwash can reduce the chance of the culture growing; she should rinse with plain water only.
The specimens should be collected on separate occasions, at least 8 hours apart and including at least one early morning sample, because spreading them out improves the diagnostic yield.
A small closed room concentrates infectious droplet nuclei, which puts the next family member to go in at risk; she should collect outdoors or in a well-ventilated area.

questions.stem: Jenny, 26, born in Cambodia, has 6 weeks of productive cough, 5 days of blood-streaked sputum, a temperature of 37.8 °C and 5 kg weight loss. Her X-ray shows right upper lobe opacification. SpO2 is 97% on room air. She is wearing a surgical mask in a separate room. What is the most appropriate next step in general practice?
options: Prescribe moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily for 5 days and review in a week
Start isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol today at weight-based doses
Arrange 3 sputum samples for AFB microscopy, culture and NAAT; phone the TB service today
Request an interferon-gamma release assay and refer if it comes back positive
questions.why: With suspected pulmonary TB, the GP collects three sputum specimens for AFB microscopy, culture and NAAT and refers urgently, by phone the same day, to the state TB service. That service confirms the diagnosis, starts treatment and organises contact tracing.
notes: A fluoroquinolone partly treats TB, which can delay the diagnosis, make sputum cultures falsely negative and select for fluoroquinolone resistance, so avoid it whenever TB is suspected.
Treatment is started by the TB service after specimens have been taken, so that culture and drug-susceptibility testing are not compromised; empirical TB treatment is not started in general practice.
An IGRA cannot tell latent from active TB and can be negative in active disease, so it does not confirm or exclude TB, and waiting for it delays urgent referral.

questions.stem: Jenny, 26, has suspected reactivation (post-primary) pulmonary TB. Her chest X-ray shows multifocal opacification in the right upper lobe and clear lower zones. Which mechanism best explains why reactivation TB favours the lung apices?
options: A high apical V/Q ratio raises alveolar PO2, which favours the aerobic Mycobacterium
Apical perfusion is the highest in the lung, so it delivers the most bacilli to the apex
Upright breathing sends most inhaled droplets to the apices rather than the bases
Low apical alveolar PO2 suppresses macrophage killing and lets the bacilli multiply
questions.why: In the upright lung, perfusion falls off toward the apex more than ventilation does, so the apical V/Q ratio is high and the alveolar PO2 is the highest in the lung. M. tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe and thrives there. Poorer apical lymphatic clearance also contributes.
notes: Because of gravity, perfusion is lowest at the apex and highest at the bases, so this gets the gradient the wrong way round.
Ventilation per unit volume is greater at the bases, which is why inhaled primary infection often lands in the mid and lower zones, not the apices.
Apical alveolar PO2 is higher, not lower, than at the bases, and the high oxygen tension favours the bacillus rather than impairing host defence.

questions.stem: Examining Jenny, 26, with suspected right upper lobe TB, you hear crackles over the upper right anterior chest. To map the right upper lobe on the front of the chest, you need its lower boundary. Which surface marking forms the inferior limit of the right upper lobe anteriorly?
options: Sternal angle, level with the 2nd costal cartilage, across to the midclavicular line
Oblique fissure, from the T3 spinous process round to the 6th costal cartilage
Lower border of the lung, along the 6th rib in the midclavicular line
Horizontal fissure, along the right 4th costal cartilage to the midaxillary line
questions.why: The horizontal fissure runs from the sternum along the right 4th costal cartilage and rib to meet the oblique fissure at the midaxillary line. It separates the right upper lobe from the middle lobe, so the anterior chest above it overlies the upper lobe.
notes: The sternal angle marks the 2nd costal cartilage and the tracheal bifurcation, which is well above the lower edge of the upper lobe; most of the anterior upper lobe lies below it.
The oblique fissure separates the upper lobe from the lower lobe posteriorly, but on the anterior chest it separates the middle lobe from the lower lobe.
The 6th rib in the midclavicular line is the inferior border of the whole lung, which lies below the middle lobe, not the upper lobe.
